title: Shoulder, Axilla & Arm
summary: Build the upper limb from the pectoral girdle to the elbow crease, including the joints and the axilla.

lessons.title: Clavicle, Scapula & Humerus Landmarks

levels.kid:
Your arm hangs from your body by a few special bones. Think of a coat hanger.

The **collarbone** (clavicle) is the long, thin bone you can feel at the bottom of your neck. It works like a strut that holds your shoulder out to the side.

The **shoulder blade** (scapula) is a flat, triangle-shaped bone on your back. It has a shallow dish where your arm bone fits, like a ball sitting on a saucer.

The **upper arm bone** (humerus) has a round ball at the top. Along it are bumps and grooves where muscles grab on and nerves travel.

Doctors learn every bump. If a bone breaks at one spot, they know which nerve nearby might get hurt.
levels.hs:
The **pectoral girdle** attaches the arm to the trunk. It is made of the **clavicle** and the **scapula**. The **humerus** is the arm bone.

**Clavicle**: an S-shaped bone. Its medial end meets the sternum, and its lateral end meets the scapula's acromion. It is the only bony connection between the upper limb and the trunk. It is the most commonly fractured bone, usually in the middle third, often from falling on the shoulder.

**Scapula** landmarks:
- **Spine**: the ridge across the back of the scapula.
- **Acromion**: the flat tip of the spine at the top of the shoulder.
- **Coracoid process**: a hook pointing forward.
- **Glenoid cavity**: the shallow socket for the humerus.
- **Supraspinous** and **infraspinous fossae**: hollows above and below the spine.

**Humerus** landmarks:
- **Head**: the ball at the top.
- **Anatomical neck**: just below the head. The **surgical neck** is a little lower and breaks more often.
- **Greater and lesser tubercles**, with the **intertubercular (bicipital) groove** between them.
- **Deltoid tuberosity**: a bump on the shaft.
- **Radial groove**: a spiral channel on the back of the shaft.
- **Medial and lateral epicondyles** at the elbow end.

Real example: a fracture of the humeral shaft can injure the radial nerve in the radial groove. The patient cannot lift the wrist, a sign called **wrist drop**.
levels.college:
Bony landmarks matter because they are attachment sites and because nerves and vessels lie against them.

**Clavicle**
- Sternal end (articulates at the sternoclavicular joint) and acromial end (acromioclavicular joint).
- Medial two-thirds convex anteriorly, lateral third concave.
- **Conoid tubercle** and **trapezoid line** underneath for the coracoclavicular ligament; **impression for the costoclavicular ligament** medially; **subclavian groove** for subclavius.
- It is the first bone to start ossifying (intramembranous, around fetal week 5–6). Its medial epiphysis is one of the last to fuse, in the 20s.
- In a midshaft fracture, sternocleidomastoid pulls the medial fragment up. The arm's weight and pectoralis major pull the lateral fragment down and in.

**Scapula**
- Lies over ribs 2–7. It has superior, medial and lateral borders and superior and inferior angles. The inferior angle is roughly at the T7 level.
- **Suprascapular notch**: the superior transverse scapular ligament bridges it. The suprascapular nerve passes below the ligament and the artery passes above it.
- **Supraglenoid** and **infraglenoid tubercles**: origins of the biceps long head and triceps long head.
- **Subscapular fossa** on the costal surface.
- The **spinoglenoid notch** connects the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae.

**Humerus**
- Head faces medially, superiorly and posteriorly. The anatomical neck is the old epiphyseal line.
- **Surgical neck**: the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery wrap around it.
- **Intertubercular groove**: the biceps long head tendon runs in it, held by the transverse humeral ligament.
- **Radial groove**: carries the radial nerve and the profunda brachii artery.
- Distal end: **capitulum** (radius) and **trochlea** (ulna); **coronoid**, **radial** and **olecranon fossae**.
- **Medial epicondyle**: the ulnar nerve passes posterior to it, the "funny bone."
- **Supracondylar ridges**.

A memory aid for nerve-bone contacts going down the humerus is **ARM**: Axillary at the surgical neck, Radial at the midshaft, ulnar at the Medial epicondyle.
levels.phd:
Clavicular development is unusual. The clavicle forms largely by **intramembranous ossification** from two primary centres, and its ends add cartilage-mediated growth. **Cleidocranial dysplasia** shows this link. It is caused by heterozygous loss of function of **RUNX2**, the master osteoblast transcription factor. It causes hypoplastic or absent clavicles, which lets patients bring their shoulders together. It also causes delayed closure of the cranial sutures and fontanelles, which are also intramembranous bone. The medial clavicular epiphysis fuses last, roughly between ages 22 and 25. Forensic age estimation uses it, staged on thin-slice CT.

The scapula has several ossification centres: the body, coracoid, acromion, inferior angle and others. If acromial centres fail to unite, the result is an **os acromiale**. It is present in about 7–8% of people and is more often bilateral than not. It can mimic a fracture on imaging and may contribute to subacromial impingement.

The **suprascapular notch** varies in shape. In the Rengachary classification, a fully ossified ligament (type VI) turns the notch into a foramen. This variant is linked to suprascapular neuropathy. The suprascapular nerve can also be compressed at the spinoglenoid notch, for example by a paralabral ganglion cyst. Compression there spares supraspinatus and weakens only infraspinatus.

The humeral head is **retroverted** about 20–30° relative to the epicondylar axis, with wide individual variation. Throwing athletes often have greater retroversion in the dominant arm. This is thought to be a developmental adaptation of the proximal physis to repeated external-rotation torque in childhood. The neck-shaft angle is about 130–135°.

About 1% of people have a **supracondylar process**, a bony spur about 5 cm above the medial epicondyle. A fibrous band, the **ligament of Struthers**, may connect it to the epicondyle. The median nerve and brachial artery can be compressed beneath this band, producing a proximal median neuropathy that can be mistaken for carpal tunnel syndrome.

The humeral shaft's radial groove is a spiral path, not a straight one. Holstein–Lewis fractures, oblique fractures of the distal third of the shaft, are classically linked to radial nerve entrapment. That is because the nerve is fixed where it pierces the lateral intermuscular septum.
levels.expert:
Clinically, these landmarks are mainly used to predict nerve injury and to plan surgical approaches safely.

**Proximal humerus fractures.** Most occur through the surgical neck in older adults with osteoporosis. The Neer classification counts displaced parts: head, shaft, greater tuberosity and lesser tuberosity. Axillary nerve injury is common, though often subclinical, so test deltoid function and regimental badge sensation before any reduction. Blood supply to the head comes mainly from the posterior circumflex humeral artery (after Hettrich's 2010 work), with the anterior circumflex contributing via the arcuate artery. A preserved posteromedial metaphyseal extension, the "calcar," predicts head viability (Hertel criteria).

**Midshaft clavicle.** Several trials, including the Canadian Orthopaedic Trauma Society trial, found lower nonunion rates and better early function with plate fixation for displaced fractures. The long-term advantage is modest. Fixation now depends on the patient, with attention to shortening, comminution and the patient's activity demands. When drilling during plating, protect the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus, which lie posteroinferior to the bone.

**Radial nerve and the humeral shaft.** Most primary radial nerve palsies after closed shaft fractures are neurapraxias and recover. Many surgeons observe them and use EMG and ultrasound if there is no recovery by about 3–4 months. Open fractures or palsy appearing after manipulation change that calculation. In the posterior approach, the nerve crosses the posterior humerus roughly midway between the acromion and the lateral epicondyle. Known distances from these palpable landmarks help guide dissection.

**Pitfalls.**
- Mistaking os acromiale or unfused physes for fractures in adolescents.
- Overlooking a posterior dislocation on a single AP film. Signs include the "lightbulb" head and loss of the half-moon overlap, so obtain an axillary view.
- Mistaking a supracondylar process for a tumour.

**Frontiers.**
- Patient-specific 3D-printed guides and CT-based planning of glenoid version and inclination for shoulder arthroplasty.
- Statistical shape models, which show that retroversion and head geometry vary too widely for standard "average" implants.
- High-resolution ultrasound to trace the radial nerve against the groove before surgery.

Open questions remain about how much the dominant arm's humeral retroversion protects throwers against injury.

keyPoints: The clavicle is the only bony strut linking the upper limb to the axial skeleton
Key scapular landmarks: spine, acromion, coracoid, glenoid, suprascapular notch
Surgical neck fractures risk the axillary nerve
Midshaft humerus fractures risk the radial nerve in the radial groove
The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle
The clavicle ossifies first, intramembranously; RUNX2 loss causes cleidocranial dysplasia

test.q: Which nerve is most at risk in a fracture of the humeral surgical neck?
test.explain: The axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery wrap around the surgical neck. The radial nerve is at risk lower, at the midshaft.

test.q: Wrist drop after a humeral shaft fracture points to injury of the:
test.explain: The radial nerve runs in the radial groove on the back of the shaft and supplies the wrist extensors.

test.q: The long head of biceps tendon runs in the:
test.explain: The bicipital (intertubercular) groove lies between the greater and lesser tubercles.

test.q: The trochlea of the humerus articulates with the:
test.explain: The trochlea meets the ulna. The capitulum meets the radius.

test.q: The 'funny bone' tingle comes from the nerve passing behind the:
test.explain: The ulnar nerve lies posterior to the medial epicondyle.

test.q: The forward-pointing hook-like process of the scapula is the:
test.explain: The coracoid points anteriorly. The acromion is the lateral end of the scapular spine.

test.q: At the suprascapular notch, the suprascapular nerve passes:
test.explain: The nerve passes below the superior transverse scapular ligament and the artery passes above it.

test.q: In a midshaft clavicle fracture, the medial fragment is pulled up by:
test.explain: Sternocleidomastoid elevates the medial fragment, while the weight of the arm drags the lateral fragment down.

test.q: The triceps long head arises from the:
test.explain: The infraglenoid tubercle gives origin to the triceps long head. The supraglenoid tubercle gives origin to the biceps long head.

test.q: What is the medical name for the collarbone?
test.explain: The clavicle is the S-shaped strut between the sternum and the acromion.

test.q: The flat lateral end of the scapular spine at the top of the shoulder is the ___.
test.explain: The acromion articulates with the clavicle at the AC joint.

test.q: The shallow socket of the scapula for the humeral head is the ___ cavity.
test.explain: The glenoid cavity forms the scapular side of the shoulder joint.

kidTest.q: Which bone is your collarbone?
kidTest.explain: The clavicle is the collarbone at the bottom of your neck.

kidTest.q: What shape is the shoulder blade?
kidTest.explain: The scapula is a flat, triangle-shaped bone on your back.

kidTest.q: What is at the top of your upper arm bone?
kidTest.explain: The humerus has a round head that fits into a shallow dish.

kidTest.q: Why do doctors learn the bumps on bones?
choices: To know which nerves are nearby
To count how old bones are
kidTest.explain: Knowing the bumps tells doctors which nerve could be hurt if a bone breaks there.

kidTest.q: The upper arm bone is the h _ _ _ _ _ s.
kidTest.explain: The humerus runs from the shoulder to the elbow.

advancedTest.q: A volleyball player has infraspinatus wasting but normal supraspinatus. The likeliest compression site is:
choices: The spinoglenoid notch from a ganglion cyst
The suprascapular notch below the ligament
The quadrangular space at the surgical neck
The radial groove at the humeral midshaft
advancedTest.explain: Compression at the spinoglenoid notch occurs after the branch to supraspinatus has left, so only infraspinatus is affected. Compression at the suprascapular notch would weaken both muscles.

advancedTest.q: A patient with absent clavicles also has delayed fontanelle closure. The unifying explanation is:
choices: A collagen I defect causing brittle bone
Premature fusion of the cranial sutures
A defect in RUNX2-driven intramembranous bone
Failed endochondral ossification of long bones
advancedTest.explain: The clavicle and skull vault both form largely by intramembranous ossification. RUNX2 haploinsufficiency (cleidocranial dysplasia) affects both.

advancedTest.q: Median neuropathy with brachial artery compression above the elbow suggests:
choices: Carpal tunnel compression at the wrist
A supracondylar process with Struthers' ligament
Ulnar nerve entrapment behind the medial epicondyle
advancedTest.explain: A ligament of Struthers from a supracondylar spur can compress the median nerve and brachial artery proximally. Carpal tunnel syndrome would not involve the artery.

advancedTest.q: Why is a distal-third oblique humeral fracture especially linked to radial nerve entrapment?
choices: The nerve runs through the intertubercular groove
The nerve is tethered where it pierces the lateral septum
The nerve lies directly on the anterior shaft there
The nerve is wrapped around the surgical neck
advancedTest.explain: In a Holstein–Lewis fracture, the radial nerve is fixed at the lateral intermuscular septum, so the fragments can trap it.

lessons.title: Pectoral, Scapular & Rotator Cuff Muscles

levels.kid:
Your shoulder is like a ball sitting on a very small, flat golf tee. That makes it great at moving in lots of directions, but easy to wobble. So your body wraps it in muscles that work like helpers holding the ball steady.

On the front of your chest is a big muscle called the **pec**. It helps you hug and push. On your back, flat muscles hold your shoulder blade against your ribs, like hands pressing a plate to a wall.

The most special helpers are four small muscles called the **rotator cuff**. They hug the ball like fingers around an orange. They twist your arm and keep the ball in its place when you throw or reach high.
levels.hs:
The shoulder is the most mobile joint in the body, so it depends on muscles for stability. They fall into three groups.

**Anterior chest (pectoral) muscles:**
- **Pectoralis major**: the big fan-shaped chest muscle. It pulls the arm across the body (adduction) and rotates it inward (medial rotation).
- **Pectoralis minor**: lies under it and pulls the shoulder blade forward and down.
- **Serratus anterior**: on the side of the ribs. It holds the scapula (shoulder blade) against the chest wall and swings it forward when you punch.

**Back-to-scapula muscles:** **trapezius**, **rhomboids** and **levator scapulae** lift, retract and steady the scapula. **Latissimus dorsi** is a broad back muscle that pulls the arm down and back, as in a pull-up.

**Scapulohumeral muscles:** the **deltoid** caps the shoulder and lifts the arm out to the side (abduction). Under it lies the **rotator cuff**, remembered as **SITS**: **S**upraspinatus, **I**nfraspinatus, **T**eres minor and **S**ubscapularis. Their tendons blend with the joint capsule and press the head of the humerus into its shallow socket.

Real example: a pitcher who throws hard for years can tear the **supraspinatus** tendon. This makes lifting the arm sideways painful and weak.
levels.college:
Shoulder muscles are grouped by attachment: **anterior axioappendicular** (trunk to limb, front), **posterior axioappendicular**, and **scapulohumeral**.

**Anterior axioappendicular**
- **Pectoralis major**: clavicular and sternocostal heads insert on the lateral lip of the intertubercular groove. It adducts and medially rotates the humerus. The clavicular head also flexes the arm. Innervation: **lateral and medial pectoral nerves**.
- **Pectoralis minor**: runs from ribs 3-5 to the coracoid process. It protracts and depresses the scapula and is a key landmark of the axilla. Nerve: medial pectoral nerve.
- **Subclavius**: anchors and depresses the clavicle. Nerve to subclavius.
- **Serratus anterior**: arises from ribs 1-8 and inserts on the medial border of the scapula. It protracts the scapula and upwardly rotates it. Nerve: **long thoracic nerve (C5-C7)**. Injury causes **winged scapula**.

**Posterior axioappendicular**
- **Trapezius** (spinal accessory nerve, CN XI): elevates, retracts and upwardly rotates the scapula.
- **Latissimus dorsi** (thoracodorsal nerve): extends, adducts and medially rotates the humerus.
- **Levator scapulae** and **rhomboids** (dorsal scapular nerve): elevate and retract the scapula and rotate it downward.

**Scapulohumeral**
- **Deltoid** (axillary nerve): abducts the arm from about 15 degrees onward. The anterior fibres flex and the posterior fibres extend.
- **Teres major** (lower subscapular nerve): adducts and medially rotates the arm.
- **Rotator cuff**:
  - **Supraspinatus** (suprascapular nerve): starts the first ~15 degrees of abduction and inserts on the greater tubercle.
  - **Infraspinatus** (suprascapular nerve): lateral rotation.
  - **Teres minor** (axillary nerve): lateral rotation.
  - **Subscapularis** (upper and lower subscapular nerves): medial rotation. It inserts on the **lesser tubercle**.

**Scapulohumeral rhythm**: during abduction, roughly 2 degrees of glenohumeral movement occur for every 1 degree of scapular rotation. Trapezius and serratus anterior form a force couple for upward rotation.
levels.phd:
Rotator cuff function is best modelled as **concavity compression**. The cuff's net force vector presses the humeral head into the shallow glenoid. The glenoid surface is only about a quarter to a third of the head's area. Pressing the head in lets the glenoid's concavity and the labrum resist translation. Inman, Saunders and Abbott's classic 1944 electromyographic studies showed that the deltoid and cuff contract together throughout elevation. They also established the roughly 2:1 scapulohumeral rhythm, although later 3D motion analysis shows that the ratio varies with arm angle and load.

The cuff works through **force couples**:
- **Transverse plane**: subscapularis anteriorly balances infraspinatus and teres minor posteriorly. Burkhart's "suspension bridge" model explains why a tear with a balanced couple (the "rotator cable" intact) can be functionally compensated.
- **Coronal plane**: the deltoid's superior shear is opposed by the inferior pull of the lower cuff.
- **Scapular upward rotation**: upper trapezius and lower serratus rotate the scapula, with lower trapezius acting about the root of the spine.

The idea that supraspinatus is the sole initiator of abduction is an oversimplification. Patients with suprascapular nerve block can still abduct, but with reduced strength and endurance.

The cuff tendons fuse with the capsule into a continuous footprint. The supraspinatus inserts on the anterior greater tubercle. Infraspinatus overlaps it more than older texts described: Mochizuki's 2008 anatomy work showed that the supraspinatus footprint is smaller than assumed. The **critical zone** near the supraspinatus insertion has relatively poor blood supply, but whether this explains degenerative tears remains debated.

**Pathophysiology debate**: Neer proposed **extrinsic impingement**, where the tendon is compressed under the coracoacromial arch. Codman and others favoured **intrinsic tendinopathy**, with age-related collagen disorganisation and tensile overload. Current evidence favours intrinsic degeneration as primary, with impingement a contributor.

Innervation follows the brachial plexus. The **suprascapular nerve** passes under the superior transverse scapular ligament and around the spinoglenoid notch. Compression at the second site denervates infraspinatus alone.
levels.expert:
Clinical localisation turns on specific tests:
- **Jobe (empty can) test**: supraspinatus.
- **External rotation lag sign** and resisted external rotation: infraspinatus.
- **Hornblower sign**: teres minor, a marker of massive posterosuperior tears.
- **Lift-off, belly-press and bear-hug tests**: subscapularis. Bear-hug is the most sensitive for upper-border tears.

Individual tests have modest specificity, so clusters of tests and imaging matter.

Asymptomatic cuff tears are extremely common with age. Ultrasound and MRI series find full-thickness tears in a substantial minority of people over 60 who have no symptoms. A tear on imaging is therefore not automatically the pain generator.

Prognosis after repair is governed by tissue quality. The **Goutallier classification** of fatty infiltration on CT/MRI and the **Patte classification** of tendon retraction both predict outcome. Fatty infiltration and muscle atrophy are largely irreversible once advanced. Arthroscopic double-row and transosseous-equivalent repairs improve footprint restoration, but retear rates rise sharply with patient age and tear size.

Options for irreparable tears include:
- Partial repair, which restores the force couples.
- **Superior capsular reconstruction** (Mihata).
- Tendon transfers, using latissimus dorsi for posterosuperior defects and pectoralis major or lower trapezius for subscapularis or external rotation loss.
- **Reverse total shoulder arthroplasty** in cuff tear arthropathy. It medialises and lowers the centre of rotation so the deltoid can elevate the arm without a functioning cuff.

For the nerve-minded:
- **Long thoracic nerve palsy**, from traction or surgery such as axillary node dissection, gives medial winging.
- **Spinal accessory palsy**, often iatrogenic after posterior triangle lymph node biopsy, gives lateral winging with shoulder droop.
- **Quadrilateral space syndrome** compresses the axillary nerve, affecting teres minor and deltoid.
- **Parsonage-Turner syndrome** (neuralgic amyotrophy) presents as severe pain followed by patchy weakness, often of serratus or the suprascapular territory.

Open questions:
- Biological augmentation (patches, platelet-rich preparations, stem-cell strategies) to recreate the graded tendon-bone enthesis. Robust evidence is still lacking.
- Whether early repair of asymptomatic tears prevents progression.
- How to rehabilitate **scapular dyskinesis** effectively.

keyPoints: Shoulder muscles: anterior and posterior axioappendicular plus scapulohumeral groups
Rotator cuff = SITS: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis
Subscapularis medially rotates; infraspinatus and teres minor laterally rotate
Serratus anterior (long thoracic nerve) holds the scapula; palsy causes winging
Deltoid (axillary nerve) abducts; supraspinatus helps start abduction
The cuff stabilises by compressing the humeral head into the glenoid

test.q: Which muscle is NOT part of the rotator cuff?
test.explain: The cuff is SITS. Teres minor belongs to the cuff, but teres major does not.

test.q: Which nerve supplies serratus anterior?
test.explain: The long thoracic nerve (C5-C7) supplies serratus anterior. The thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus dorsi.

test.q: Damage to the nerve of serratus anterior typically produces:
test.explain: Without serratus, the medial border of the scapula lifts off the chest wall.

test.q: Which cuff muscle is the main medial rotator of the humerus?
test.explain: Subscapularis inserts on the lesser tubercle and medially rotates. Infraspinatus and teres minor rotate laterally.

test.q: Which nerve supplies both the deltoid and teres minor?
test.explain: The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor. The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus.

test.q: Pectoralis major mainly performs which actions on the arm?
test.explain: Pectoralis major adducts and medially rotates the humerus. Its clavicular head also flexes.

test.q: The trapezius is supplied by which nerve?
test.explain: Trapezius is innervated by cranial nerve XI, the spinal accessory nerve.

test.q: The scapulohumeral rhythm during abduction is roughly:
choices: Scapular movement with no humeral motion
test.explain: About 2 degrees of glenohumeral motion occur per 1 degree of scapular rotation, although the ratio varies.

test.q: Pectoralis minor inserts onto which scapular landmark?
test.explain: Pectoralis minor runs from ribs 3-5 to the coracoid process.

test.q: Which cuff muscle helps start abduction and is the one most often torn?
test.explain: Supraspinatus initiates about the first 15 degrees of abduction and is frequently torn.

test.q: Latissimus dorsi is supplied by the ___ nerve.
test.explain: The thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus dorsi, which extends, adducts and medially rotates the arm.

test.q: The four cuff muscles are remembered by the mnemonic ___.
test.explain: SITS stands for Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor and Subscapularis.

kidTest.q: What is the shoulder like?
choices: A ball on a small flat tee
A box with a tight lid
kidTest.explain: It moves a lot but needs muscles to keep it steady.

kidTest.q: What does the big chest muscle help you do?
kidTest.explain: The pec pulls your arms in and forward.

kidTest.q: How many small muscles make up the rotator cuff?
kidTest.explain: Four small muscles hug the ball of the shoulder.

kidTest.q: What do the back muscles do for the shoulder blade?
kidTest.explain: They press the shoulder blade flat, like hands holding a plate to a wall.

kidTest.q: The rotator ___ keeps your shoulder ball in place. (Hint: c _ _ _)
kidTest.explain: The rotator cuff hugs and steadies the shoulder joint.

advancedTest.q: Why can some patients with a large supraspinatus tear still elevate the arm well?
choices: Balanced front-back force couples still compress the head
Teres major takes over the initiation of abduction from it
The glenoid socket enlarges to compensate for the lost tendon
The deltoid alone fully centres the humeral head in the socket
advancedTest.explain: In Burkhart's suspension-bridge model, an intact subscapularis-infraspinatus couple preserves concavity compression despite the tear.

advancedTest.q: Isolated infraspinatus wasting with normal supraspinatus suggests compression at the:
advancedTest.explain: At the spinoglenoid notch, the suprascapular nerve has already given its branches to supraspinatus, so only infraspinatus is affected.

advancedTest.q: A reverse total shoulder arthroplasty restores elevation in cuff tear arthropathy mainly by:
choices: Medialising and lowering the centre of rotation
Fusing the scapula firmly to the thoracic wall for stability
Converting latissimus dorsi into the main abductor of the arm
Stimulating the torn cuff tendons to regrow onto the bone
advancedTest.explain: Shifting the centre of rotation lengthens the deltoid's lever arm, so it can elevate the arm without a cuff.

advancedTest.q: Why is advanced Goutallier-grade fatty infiltration a poor prognostic sign for repair?
choices: It shows tendon fluid that resolves quickly after surgery
It indicates the glenoid labrum is intact and healthy
The muscle damage largely persists after repair
It means the axillary nerve supplying it is severed
advancedTest.explain: Fatty infiltration and atrophy rarely recover, so even a healed tendon drives weak muscle and retears are more likely.

lessons.title: Glenohumeral, Acromioclavicular & Sternoclavicular Joints

levels.kid:
Your shoulder is not just one joint. It is a team of three joints working together.

The biggest is the **shoulder joint** itself. The round top of your arm bone sits in a small, shallow cup on your shoulder blade. Think of a golf ball sitting on a golf tee. That is why your arm can swing in big circles!

But a ball on a tee can fall off easily. So muscles and strong straps called **ligaments** hold it in place.

The second joint links your collarbone to the top of your shoulder blade. The third links your collarbone to your breastbone in the middle of your chest. That little joint is the only bony link between your whole arm and your body!
levels.hs:
The shoulder complex includes three true joints that let the arm move more freely than any other part of the body.

- **Glenohumeral (GH) joint**: the head of the humerus meets the **glenoid cavity** of the scapula. It is a ball-and-socket **synovial joint**. The socket is very shallow, so it trades stability for range of motion. A ring of cartilage called the **glenoid labrum** deepens it. The **rotator cuff** muscles and the joint capsule help hold the head in place.
- **Acromioclavicular (AC) joint**: the lateral end of the clavicle meets the acromion of the scapula. It is held mainly by the **coracoclavicular ligaments**, which run from the clavicle down to the coracoid process.
- **Sternoclavicular (SC) joint**: the medial end of the clavicle meets the sternum and first rib cartilage. A disc of cartilage inside makes it very strong. It is the only bony joint attaching the upper limb to the trunk.

Real example: the GH joint is the most commonly dislocated major joint in the body. Usually the humeral head pops out forward and downward (**anterior dislocation**), often when the arm is raised and twisted outward, as in a fall or a tackle. Because the axillary nerve wraps around the humerus nearby, doctors check skin sensation over the shoulder muscle after a dislocation.
levels.college:
**Glenohumeral joint**: a multiaxial ball-and-socket synovial joint. The humeral head has roughly three to four times the surface area of the glenoid, so only part of it contacts the socket at any moment.
- **Static stabilizers**: the fibrocartilaginous **glenoid labrum**, a loose fibrous capsule, and the **glenohumeral ligaments** (superior, middle, inferior). These are thickenings of the anterior capsule. The **inferior glenohumeral ligament** is the main restraint against anterior dislocation when the arm is abducted and externally rotated. The **coracohumeral ligament** reinforces the top.
- **Dynamic stabilizers**: the rotator cuff (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis) presses the head into the glenoid. The **long head of biceps** tendon starts at the supraglenoid tubercle and labrum and runs inside the capsule, though it stays outside the synovial membrane.
- **Weak point**: the capsule is thinnest inferiorly, where no cuff tendon supports it. That is why the head escapes anteroinferiorly.
- **Coracoacromial arch** (acromion, coracoacromial ligament, coracoid) forms a roof above the head. The **subacromial bursa** lets the supraspinatus glide under it.

**Acromioclavicular joint**: a plane synovial joint, often with an incomplete disc. The weak AC ligament controls horizontal movement. The coracoclavicular ligament, made of the **conoid** (medial) and **trapezoid** (lateral) parts, suspends the scapula from the clavicle and resists upward displacement of the clavicle. Falls onto the point of the shoulder cause an **AC separation**. Torn coracoclavicular ligaments give a visible step.

**Sternoclavicular joint**: a saddle-type synovial joint with an **articular disc** that splits it into two cavities. The anterior and posterior sternoclavicular ligaments, the interclavicular ligament and the **costoclavicular ligament** stabilize it. It allows elevation, depression, protraction, retraction and rotation of the clavicle. Scapular movement depends on it.

Innervation follows **Hilton's law**: the nerves to the muscles crossing a joint also supply the joint. For the GH joint these are the suprascapular, axillary and lateral pectoral nerves.
levels.phd:
Stability at the glenohumeral joint comes from several mechanisms that work at different positions.

**Concavity-compression**: cuff forces push the humeral head into the labrum-deepened glenoid. The labrum adds roughly 50% to glenoid depth, and its loss markedly reduces the force needed to translate the head. In mid-range, when the ligaments are lax, concavity-compression dominates. At end-range the capsuloligamentous restraints take over.

**Position-dependent ligament roles**:
- **SGHL** and the **coracohumeral ligament** resist inferior translation in adduction. Both lie in the **rotator interval**, between supraspinatus and subscapularis.
- **MGHL** resists anterior translation at mid-abduction. It is variably absent. The **Buford complex** is a normal variant: a cord-like MGHL with an absent anterosuperior labrum. Mistaking it for a tear is a classic pitfall.
- **IGHL complex** is a hammock with anterior and posterior bands and an axillary pouch. It is the key restraint in abduction with external rotation, the apprehension position.

**Negative intra-articular pressure** and adhesion-cohesion in the sealed capsule add modest resistance to inferior subluxation. Venting the capsule increases translation in cadaver studies.

**Lesions after anterior dislocation**:
- **Bankart lesion**: the anteroinferior labrum and IGHL avulse from the glenoid rim. A **bony Bankart** includes a rim fracture.
- **Hill-Sachs lesion**: an impaction defect on the posterolateral humeral head, made when the head strikes the anterior glenoid rim.
- The **glenoid track** concept (Yamamoto, Itoi): a Hill-Sachs lesion is "off-track" if it can engage the glenoid rim in abduction with external rotation. Combined bipolar bone loss predicts recurrence.

**Scapulohumeral rhythm**: Inman's 1944 work described about 2:1 glenohumeral-to-scapulothoracic motion during elevation. Later 3D kinematic studies show the ratio varies with plane and phase. Scapular upward rotation requires clavicular elevation and posterior axial rotation at the SC joint, coupled through the AC joint and the coracoclavicular ligaments. Clavicular rotation is limited if the clavicle is fixed to the coracoid, as by a rigid screw.

**AC biomechanics**: sectioning studies (Fukuda 1986) showed the AC capsule limits small anteroposterior displacement. The conoid mainly resists superior displacement, and the trapezoid resists axial compression.
levels.expert:
**Imaging and classification.** AC injuries use the Rockwood classification, types I to VI. Type I is a sprain. Type II tears the AC ligaments. Type III also tears the coracoclavicular ligaments, giving roughly 25 to 100% coracoclavicular widening. Types IV (posterior into trapezius), V (marked superior displacement with deltotrapezial fascia stripping) and VI (subcoracoid) are generally surgical. Type III management remains debated. Randomized data have not shown clear superiority of early fixation for most patients, so many centers start nonoperatively and reserve surgery for persistent dysfunction, horizontal instability or overhead athletes. Zanca views (cephalic tilt) and cross-body adduction views help assess horizontal instability.

**SC joint.** Posterior SC dislocation is uncommon but dangerous. The medial clavicle can press on the brachiocephalic vessels, trachea or esophagus. Plain films miss it, so CT is the study of choice. Reduction is often done with a thoracic surgeon available. In patients under about 25, the medial clavicular physis, one of the last to fuse, may fail instead. These **physeal injuries** mimic dislocations. Avoid transfixing SC pins, since migration toward the great vessels has been reported.

**Glenohumeral instability decisions.** Recurrence after a first anterior dislocation is highest in young, male, contact athletes. Glenoid bone loss beyond a critical threshold, historically about 20 to 25% and now considered lower (around 13 to 17% "subcritical" loss), predicts failure of arthroscopic Bankart repair. Options then include the **Latarjet** coracoid transfer, which works through a bony block, the conjoint tendon "sling" and capsular repair, or free bone block grafts. Off-track lesions may need **remplissage**, filling the Hill-Sachs defect with infraspinatus tendon. Instability severity scores such as the ISIS score help guide these choices.

**Pitfalls.** Posterior dislocation, classically after seizures or electrocution, is missed on AP films. Look for the "light bulb" sign and get an axillary view. In older patients, first dislocation often comes with a rotator cuff tear or axillary nerve palsy rather than a labral lesion. Check the deltoid both before and after reduction.

**Open questions.** These include the best fixation for AC reconstruction (anatomic coracoclavicular grafts versus suture buttons), the role of early stabilization after a first dislocation, and whether 3D bone-loss measurement improves outcomes.

keyPoints: Glenohumeral joint: shallow ball-and-socket that trades stability for mobility
Labrum, capsule and glenohumeral ligaments are static stabilizers; the rotator cuff is dynamic
Inferior glenohumeral ligament resists anterior dislocation in abduction with external rotation
AC joint stability depends mainly on the conoid and trapezoid (coracoclavicular) ligaments
SC joint is a saddle joint with a disc: the only bony link of limb to trunk
Anterior dislocation causes Bankart and Hill-Sachs lesions and risks axillary nerve injury

test.q: What type of joint is the glenohumeral joint?
test.explain: The humeral head (ball) articulates with the glenoid cavity (socket), allowing multiaxial movement.

test.q: Which structure deepens the glenoid cavity?
test.explain: The fibrocartilaginous labrum rims and deepens the shallow glenoid. The articular disc belongs to the SC joint.

test.q: In which direction does the humeral head usually dislocate?
test.explain: The capsule is weakest inferiorly with no cuff support, so most dislocations are anterior and inferior.

test.q: Which nerve is classically checked after an anterior shoulder dislocation?
test.explain: The axillary nerve wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus near the inferior capsule, so it can be stretched.

test.q: Which ligament mainly holds the clavicle down at the AC joint?
test.explain: The conoid and trapezoid parts of the coracoclavicular ligament suspend the scapula and resist upward clavicle displacement.

test.q: The sternoclavicular joint is described as which type of synovial joint?
test.explain: The SC joint is a saddle-type joint with an articular disc. The AC joint is the plane joint.

test.q: Which ligament resists anterior dislocation with the arm abducted and externally rotated?
test.explain: The inferior glenohumeral ligament complex acts as a hammock that is the key restraint in abduction with external rotation.

test.q: What is a Hill-Sachs lesion?
choices: A tear of the anteroinferior glenoid labrum
A fracture through the tip of the coracoid process
A rupture of both coracoclavicular ligament parts
A posterolateral humeral head impaction defect
test.explain: The head strikes the anterior glenoid rim during dislocation. A labral avulsion is a Bankart lesion instead.

test.q: Hilton's law states that a joint is supplied by nerves that:
choices: Supply the skin directly over it
Supply the muscles crossing that joint
Run through the joint capsule cavity
Leave the spinal cord at one level
test.explain: Hence the GH joint is supplied by the suprascapular, axillary and lateral pectoral nerves.

test.q: The coracoclavicular ligament has a medial conoid part and a lateral ___ part.
test.explain: Conoid is medial; trapezoid is lateral.

test.q: What is the name of the avulsion of the anteroinferior labrum seen after anterior dislocation?
test.explain: A Bankart lesion is the labrum and IGHL pulled off the glenoid rim. A bony Bankart includes a rim fracture.

test.q: The ___ joint is the only bony articulation linking the upper limb to the trunk.
test.explain: All other attachments of the limb to the trunk are muscular.

kidTest.q: How many joints work together in the shoulder in this lesson?
kidTest.explain: The shoulder joint, the collarbone-to-shoulder-blade joint, and the collarbone-to-breastbone joint.

kidTest.q: The shoulder joint is like a golf ball sitting on a what?
kidTest.explain: The socket is shallow like a tee, so the arm can swing in big circles.

kidTest.q: Why can the shoulder pop out easily?
kidTest.explain: A shallow cup gives lots of movement but less hold.

kidTest.q: Which bones meet at the joint in the middle of your chest?
kidTest.explain: That small joint links the collarbone to the breastbone and connects the whole arm to the body.

kidTest.q: Strong straps that hold joints together are called l _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Ligaments are tough bands connecting bone to bone.

advancedTest.q: Why does concavity-compression matter most in mid-range glenohumeral motion?
choices: The labrum is absent during the mid-range of arm elevation
Ligaments are lax there, so cuff compression gives stability
Intra-articular pressure turns strongly positive in the mid-range
The coracoacromial arch locks the humeral head during mid-range
advancedTest.explain: Ligaments tighten mainly at end-range. In mid-range, cuff forces pressing the head into the glenoid provide most of the stability.

advancedTest.q: On MRI, a cord-like MGHL with an absent anterosuperior labrum should most likely be interpreted as:
choices: A superior labral tear from biceps traction
An acute Bankart lesion needing repair
A Hill-Sachs lesion seen on the glenoid side
A Buford complex, a normal anatomic variant
advancedTest.explain: The Buford complex is a normal variant. Mistaking it for a tear and repairing it is a classic pitfall.

advancedTest.q: A young contact athlete has an off-track Hill-Sachs lesion and significant glenoid bone loss. Why is isolated arthroscopic Bankart repair a poor fit?
choices: Bankart repair mainly treats posterior instability after seizures
Arthroscopy is contraindicated whenever the axillary nerve has been tested
Labral repair causes the coracoclavicular ligaments to rupture
Soft-tissue repair does not address the bony defects driving engagement and recurrence
advancedTest.explain: Bipolar bone loss lets the lesion engage the rim. Bony procedures such as Latarjet, with or without remplissage, address this.

advancedTest.q: A trauma patient under 25 appears to have a posterior SC dislocation. Which interpretation and step are most appropriate?
choices: Transfixing pins across the SC joint are the preferred first-line treatment
Anterior and posterior SC injuries carry a similarly low risk to vessels
It is likely a benign sprain, so plain radiographs alone will suffice
May be a medial clavicular physeal injury; get CT, check mediastinum
advancedTest.explain: The medial clavicular physis fuses late, so physeal injuries mimic dislocations. Posterior displacement threatens the great vessels and airway, so CT is the study of choice.

lessons.title: The Axilla: Walls, Contents & Axillary Artery

levels.kid:
Lift your arm and look at your armpit. Doctors call it the **axilla**. It looks small, but it is like a busy tunnel between your neck and your arm.

The tunnel has walls made of muscles and bones. Your chest muscle is at the front. Your shoulder blade muscles are at the back. Your ribs are on the inside.

Inside the tunnel run big pipes and cables. A large **artery** carries blood to your arm. A **vein** brings blood back. Thick **nerves** carry messages so your arm can move and feel. Little bean-shaped **lymph nodes** catch germs like tiny filters.

Soft fat wraps around everything like bubble wrap, so it can all stretch when you swing your arm.
levels.hs:
The **axilla** (armpit) is a pyramid-shaped space where the neck connects to the upper limb. All the major structures headed for the arm pass through it.

Its boundaries:
- **Apex** (top): the **cervicoaxillary canal**, an opening bounded by the clavicle, first rib and the top edge of the scapula. Vessels and nerves enter here from the neck.
- **Base**: the armpit skin and fascia.
- **Anterior wall**: pectoralis major and pectoralis minor.
- **Posterior wall**: subscapularis, teres major and latissimus dorsi.
- **Medial wall**: serratus anterior over the ribs.
- **Lateral wall**: the narrow intertubercular groove of the humerus.

Contents:
- **Axillary artery** and **axillary vein**
- The cords and branches of the **brachial plexus**, the nerve network supplying the arm
- **Axillary lymph nodes**
- Fat that cushions everything

The artery, the nerve cords and some fat are wrapped together in the **axillary sheath**, a tube of connective tissue continuous with fascia from the neck.

Real example: the axillary lymph nodes drain about 75% of lymph from the breast. That is why surgeons check these nodes in breast cancer. Cancer cells that leave the breast often reach them first.
levels.college:
The axilla is a truncated pyramid transmitting the neurovascular supply of the upper limb.

**Walls**
- Anterior: pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, subclavius, clavipectoral fascia
- Posterior: subscapularis, teres major, latissimus dorsi (the posterior axillary fold)
- Medial: serratus anterior and the upper ribs
- Lateral: intertubercular sulcus
- Apex: cervicoaxillary canal (clavicle, rib 1, superior scapular border)

**Axillary artery.** It continues the subclavian artery at the lateral border of rib 1 and becomes the brachial artery at the inferior border of teres major. **Pectoralis minor** crosses it and divides it into three parts. Each part's number matches its number of branches.
- Part 1: **superior thoracic** artery
- Part 2: **thoracoacromial** trunk and **lateral thoracic** artery
- Part 3: **subscapular** artery (which gives circumflex scapular and thoracodorsal branches), and the **anterior** and **posterior circumflex humeral** arteries

Mnemonic: "Screw The Lawyer, Save A Patient."

**Brachial plexus relations.** The lateral, medial and posterior cords are named by their position around part 2 of the artery. Their terminal branches (musculocutaneous, median, ulnar, radial, axillary) form around part 3. The median nerve's two roots make an "M" in front of the artery.

**Axillary vein.** It forms from the basilic vein (and brachial veins) and becomes the subclavian vein at rib 1. It lies anteromedial to the artery, outside the axillary sheath, and receives the cephalic vein.

**Lymph nodes.** There are five groups: pectoral (anterior), subscapular (posterior), humeral (lateral), central and apical. Drainage converges on the apical nodes and then the subclavian trunk.

Nerves on the walls include the **long thoracic nerve** on serratus anterior, the **thoracodorsal nerve** with its artery to latissimus dorsi, and the **intercostobrachial nerve** crossing the space.
levels.phd:
Developmentally, the axillary artery arises from the seventh cervical intersegmental artery, which forms the subclavian-axillary-brachial axis. Its branching pattern varies widely. Cadaver studies report that the textbook six-branch pattern holds in only a minority of limbs. Common variants:
- A **common subscapular-circumflex humeral trunk**
- The lateral thoracic artery arising from the thoracoacromial or subscapular arteries
- A **superficial brachial artery** or high division of the brachial artery, usually originating from the third part. It passes superficial to the median nerve roots and can mimic a duplicated vessel on imaging.

**Collateral circulation.** The **scapular anastomosis** links the subclavian artery (suprascapular and dorsal scapular arteries) to the third part of the axillary artery (circumflex scapular artery, via the subscapular). Ligating the axillary artery between the thyrocervical trunk and the subscapular origin is usually tolerated, because flow reverses down the subscapular artery. Ligation distal to the subscapular artery, but proximal to the profunda brachii, carries far greater ischemic risk.

**Fascial architecture.** The axillary sheath comes from the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia. Internal septa divide it into compartments, which may explain the patchy spread of local anesthetic seen in some axillary blocks. The **clavipectoral fascia** encloses subclavius and pectoralis minor. Its costocoracoid membrane is pierced by four structures: the cephalic vein, the thoracoacromial artery, the lateral pectoral nerve and lymphatics. The suspensory ligament of the axilla pulls the skin up when the arm is abducted, which creates the hollow.

**Lymphatic topology.** Surgeons classify axillary nodes as **Berg levels** relative to pectoralis minor:
- Level I: lateral to the muscle
- Level II: deep to it
- Level III: medial to it, toward the apex

**Interpectoral (Rotter) nodes** lie between the pectoral muscles. Spread usually proceeds stepwise, but "skip metastases" to level III without level I involvement occur in a small fraction of patients. This complicates the logic of staged dissection.

**Wall nerves at risk.** The long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) lies superficial to serratus anterior, on the medial wall. The thoracodorsal nerve (C6–C8) runs with the thoracodorsal artery on the posterior wall. Both lie within the operative field of the axilla.
levels.expert:
**Breast surgery.** Axillary surgery has shifted dramatically in recent decades. **Sentinel lymph node biopsy** uses radioisotope and/or blue dye, and newer methods use superparamagnetic iron oxide or indocyanine green fluorescence. It has largely replaced routine axillary lymph node dissection (ALND) for clinically node-negative breast cancer.

Trials have narrowed the role of ALND:
- ACOSOG Z0011 showed that selected patients with one to two positive sentinel nodes who undergo breast-conserving surgery plus whole-breast radiotherapy can safely omit ALND.
- AMAROS showed that axillary radiotherapy matches ALND for local control with less lymphedema.
- SOUND and INSEMA (2023–2024) suggest that even sentinel biopsy may be omitted in selected low-risk older patients.

**Pitfalls during dissection:**
- Injury to the **long thoracic nerve** paralyzes serratus anterior and causes medial scapular winging.
- Injury to the **thoracodorsal nerve** weakens latissimus dorsi and compromises latissimus flap reconstruction.
- Sacrificing the **intercostobrachial nerve** causes numbness or chronic pain in the medial arm. This is a major contributor to post-mastectomy pain syndrome.
- Lymphedema follows level III clearance more often. Axillary reverse mapping, and lymphaticovenous anastomosis performed at the time of surgery, aim to reduce it.

**Vascular and trauma considerations.** The axillary artery is relatively tethered by its branches. Anterior shoulder dislocation and proximal humeral fractures, especially in the elderly, can cause intimal tears and delayed thrombosis. A palpable radial pulse does not exclude injury, because collaterals can preserve distal flow. CT angiography is warranted if suspicion persists. Penetrating injuries often involve the brachial plexus as well, because the cords are so close to the artery.

The artery is also an access route. Axillary artery cannulation is used for cardiopulmonary bypass and for transcatheter aortic valve implantation when femoral access is unsuitable. Its first part is preferred, though brachial plexus injury and hematoma that compresses the plexus within the sheath are recognized complications.

**Anesthesia.** Ultrasound-guided axillary block targets the median, ulnar and radial nerves around the artery. The musculocutaneous nerve often lies separately within coracobrachialis and needs its own injection.

**Open question.** It remains unclear how far fascial compartmentalization of the sheath versus individual anatomical variation explains inconsistent block spread.

keyPoints: The axilla is a pyramid with an apex, a base and four walls
Pectorals form the anterior wall; subscapularis, teres major and latissimus dorsi form the posterior wall
The axillary artery runs from the lateral border of rib 1 to the inferior border of teres major
Pectoralis minor divides the artery into parts with 1, 2 and 3 branches
Brachial plexus cords are named by their position around the second part of the artery
Axillary nodes drain most breast lymph; sentinel biopsy has largely replaced routine full dissection

test.q: Which muscle forms part of the anterior wall of the axilla?
test.explain: Pectoralis major and minor form the anterior wall. Serratus anterior forms the medial wall; teres major and subscapularis form the posterior wall.

test.q: The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery at the:
test.explain: The artery begins at the lateral border of rib 1 and becomes the brachial artery at the inferior border of teres major.

test.q: Which muscle divides the axillary artery into three parts?
test.explain: Pectoralis minor crosses in front of the artery. The segments above, behind and below it are parts 1, 2 and 3.

test.q: Which artery arises from the first part of the axillary artery?
test.explain: Part 1 has a single branch, the superior thoracic artery. Thoracoacromial and lateral thoracic come from part 2; subscapular comes from part 3.

test.q: Brachial plexus cords are named for their position relative to:
choices: The second part of the artery
test.explain: The lateral, medial and posterior cords are named by where they sit around the second part of the axillary artery.

test.q: The medial wall of the axilla is formed mainly by:
test.explain: Serratus anterior covering the upper ribs forms the medial wall. The groove is lateral, and the fascia is part of the anterior wall.

test.q: Which nerve lies on serratus anterior and is at risk during axillary surgery?
test.explain: The long thoracic nerve runs on the medial wall over serratus anterior. Injury to it causes scapular winging.

test.q: About what proportion of breast lymph drains to the axillary nodes?
test.explain: Roughly 75% of breast lymph drains to the axillary nodes. This is why they matter so much in breast cancer.

test.q: Where does the axillary vein lie relative to the axillary artery?
test.explain: The axillary vein lies anteromedial to the artery and outside the axillary sheath.

test.q: The opening at the apex of the axilla, bounded by the clavicle, first rib and scapula, is the cervico___ canal.
test.explain: Structures enter the axilla from the neck through the cervicoaxillary canal.

test.q: Which branch of the third part of the axillary artery gives rise to the thoracodorsal artery?
test.explain: The subscapular artery divides into the circumflex scapular and thoracodorsal arteries.

test.q: The axillary artery and brachial plexus cords are wrapped together in the axillary ___.
test.explain: The axillary sheath comes from the deep cervical fascia and encloses the artery and the plexus.

kidTest.q: What is the axilla?
kidTest.explain: The axilla is the doctor word for the armpit.

kidTest.q: What does the big artery in the armpit carry?
kidTest.explain: The artery carries blood to the arm.

kidTest.q: What do the lymph nodes in the armpit do?
kidTest.explain: Lymph nodes act like little filters that catch germs.

kidTest.q: What carries messages so your arm can move?
kidTest.explain: Nerves carry messages between the arm and the body.

kidTest.q: Which chest part forms the inner wall of the armpit? (r _ _ s)
kidTest.explain: The ribs, covered by muscle, form the inner wall.

advancedTest.q: Why is ligating the axillary artery proximal to the subscapular origin usually better tolerated than ligating it distal to that origin?
choices: The brachial plexus releases factors that dilate distal vessels
The axillary vein takes over arterial supply to the arm
Scapular anastomoses can refill the subscapular artery retrogradely
The thoracoacromial trunk gives direct supply to the brachial artery
advancedTest.explain: Subclavian branches feed the scapular anastomosis, which can reverse flow down the subscapular artery into the distal axillary artery. A distal ligation bypasses this route.

advancedTest.q: A patient with a proximal humeral fracture has a palpable radial pulse. Why might axillary artery injury still be present?
choices: Collateral flow can maintain distal pulses despite injury
The radial artery arises above the fracture site
Fractures rarely lie near the axillary artery
Radial pulses reflect venous return in the forearm
advancedTest.explain: Collaterals can preserve distal flow despite an intimal tear, so imaging is needed if suspicion persists.

advancedTest.q: During an axillary block the hand is numb, but elbow flexion is still strong. The likeliest explanation is that:
choices: Local anesthetic entered the axillary vein instead
The median nerve roots were above the injection
The radial nerve was spared inside its own sheath
The musculocutaneous nerve lay apart in coracobrachialis
advancedTest.explain: The musculocutaneous nerve, which supplies the elbow flexors, often leaves the sheath early within coracobrachialis and needs a separate injection.

advancedTest.q: In Z0011-type patients, omitting full axillary dissection mainly reduces which harm?
advancedTest.explain: Full axillary dissection raises the risk of lymphedema and of injury to nerves such as the intercostobrachial nerve. Trials showed it could be avoided in selected patients without worse outcomes.

lessons.title: Arm Compartments & the Cubital Fossa

levels.kid:
Your upper arm is like a sandwich with two fillings. A thin wall made of tough tissue splits it into a **front room** and a **back room**.

The front room holds muscles that **bend** your elbow, like the biceps you flex to show off. The back room holds the **triceps**, which **straightens** your elbow.

Each room has its own nerve, like its own electric wire. The front muscles get one wire, and the back muscle gets another.

At the bend of your elbow there is a little hollow called the **cubital fossa**. It is like a hallway where a big blood tube and a nerve pass through to reach your forearm. That is why nurses often take blood from veins just in front of your elbow bend.
levels.hs:
The arm (the part between shoulder and elbow) is wrapped in a sleeve of tough connective tissue called **deep fascia**. Two sheets of it, the **medial and lateral intermuscular septa**, attach to the humerus and divide the arm into two **compartments**:

- **Anterior (flexor) compartment**: biceps brachii, brachialis and coracobrachialis. These mainly flex the elbow or shoulder. They are supplied by the **musculocutaneous nerve**.
- **Posterior (extensor) compartment**: triceps brachii (and the small anconeus nearby). It extends the elbow and is supplied by the **radial nerve**.

The main artery is the **brachial artery**, which runs down the inside of the arm beside the median nerve. The **profunda brachii** (deep artery of the arm) travels with the radial nerve around the back of the humerus.

The **cubital fossa** is a triangular hollow in front of the elbow. From lateral to medial, its main contents are the **biceps tendon, brachial artery and median nerve**. A memory trick: "TAN" (Tendon, Artery, Nerve). Over its roof lies the **median cubital vein**, a common place for drawing blood.

Real example: when you measure blood pressure, the stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery just medial to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa.
levels.college:
**Compartments.** The brachial fascia and the medial and lateral intermuscular septa create two osteofascial compartments.

**Anterior compartment** (musculocutaneous nerve, C5-C7):
- **Coracobrachialis**: coracoid process to mid-humerus; flexes and adducts the shoulder. The musculocutaneous nerve pierces it.
- **Biceps brachii**: long head from the supraglenoid tubercle, short head from the coracoid; inserts on the radial tuberosity and, via the **bicipital aponeurosis**, into forearm fascia. It is the chief **supinator** of the flexed forearm and a strong elbow flexor.
- **Brachialis**: anterior distal humerus to the coronoid process and ulnar tuberosity; the pure workhorse flexor of the elbow. The lateral part also receives radial nerve fibres.

**Posterior compartment** (radial nerve, C6-C8):
- **Triceps brachii**: long head from the infraglenoid tubercle (it crosses the shoulder); lateral and medial heads from the posterior humerus, above and below the **radial groove**. It inserts on the olecranon.

**Neurovascular course.**
- The **brachial artery** continues the axillary artery at the inferior border of teres major. It runs medially, crossed by the median nerve (lateral to medial) mid-arm, and ends in the cubital fossa by dividing into radial and ulnar arteries.
- The **radial nerve** and profunda brachii spiral in the radial groove; the **ulnar nerve** pierces the medial septum and passes behind the medial epicondyle.

**Cubital fossa.**
- Boundaries: a line between the epicondyles (superior), **pronator teres** (medial), **brachioradialis** (lateral).
- Floor: brachialis and supinator. Roof: fascia reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis, with the median cubital vein superficial to it.
- Contents, lateral to medial: radial nerve (deep, under brachioradialis), biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve.

The bicipital aponeurosis helps protect the artery and median nerve during venipuncture.
levels.phd:
The arm compartments reflect embryology. Limb-bud mesoderm splits into dorsal and ventral muscle masses. Ventral (flexor) muscles are innervated by anterior divisions of the brachial plexus, which form the lateral and medial cords. The **musculocutaneous nerve** arises from the lateral cord. Dorsal (extensor) masses receive posterior divisions, which form the posterior cord and the **radial nerve**. This explains why the ventral brachialis is mostly musculocutaneous, while its lateral strip is often radial: it borders the dorsal territory. The brachioradialis is a forearm extensor-group muscle by innervation, although it acts as an elbow flexor.

**Biomechanics.** Biceps supination torque is greatest with the elbow near 90 degrees of flexion. There the tendon approaches the radial tuberosity perpendicularly and its moment arm about the radioulnar axis is largest. Brachialis acts across the humeroulnar joint, so its flexion contribution is independent of forearm rotation. Electromyographic work, building on Basmajian's classic studies, shows that brachialis is active in almost all flexion, while biceps recruitment rises with supination and load.

**Variation.** A **superficial brachial artery** or high bifurcation of the brachial artery (high radial origin) occurs in a substantial minority of limbs, commonly cited at roughly 10-20%. A **supracondylar process** with a fibrous ligament of Struthers can tether the median nerve and brachial artery. The musculocutaneous and median nerves are frequently linked by communicating branches. This alters expected deficits after injury.

**Radial groove.** The radial nerve contacts bone in the spiral groove between the lateral and medial triceps heads. It then pierces the lateral intermuscular septum about 10 cm proximal to the lateral epicondyle. Branches to the medial and lateral triceps heads may arise proximal to the groove. This is why mid-shaft injury often spares elbow extension while causing wrist drop.

**Fascial mechanics.** The septa are relatively compliant, and the anterior and posterior compartments communicate in places. This partly explains why arm compartment syndrome is far rarer than forearm or leg syndromes.
levels.expert:
**Mid-shaft humeral fractures** carry a radial nerve palsy rate commonly reported around 10-12%, highest with distal-third spiral (Holstein-Lewis) patterns. Most closed-fracture palsies are neurapraxias that recover. Many surgeons therefore observe and re-examine, using ultrasound or EMG at about 3-4 months, rather than explore early. Open fractures, or palsy appearing after manipulation, push toward exploration. In anterolateral and posterior surgical approaches, the radial nerve must be identified where it crosses the posterior humerus and where it pierces the lateral septum. The lower lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm is a useful guide back to it.

**Supracondylar fractures in children** are the classic cubital fossa emergency. Extension-type fractures displace the proximal fragment anteriorly, where it can tent or trap the brachial artery and median nerve. Anterior interosseous nerve palsy, with loss of the thumb and index finger "OK" sign, is the most common nerve deficit. A "pink, pulseless hand" after reduction remains debated: watchful observation versus vascular exploration. Volkmann ischemic contracture of the forearm flexors is the feared late result of missed ischemia.

**Distal biceps tendon rupture** mostly affects middle-aged men with eccentric loading. The hook test (Hook test of O'Driscoll) is highly sensitive. An intact bicipital aponeurosis can mask retraction. Repair restores supination strength in particular. The **lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve**, the terminal musculocutaneous branch emerging lateral to the tendon, is the most frequently injured structure in anterior repair. The posterior interosseous nerve is at risk with deep or two-incision approaches.

**Venous access pitfalls.** Medial antecubital veins overlie the brachial artery and median nerve. Deep or medial needle passes risk arterial puncture or median nerve injury, a recognized medicolegal problem.

**Nerve transfers.** In upper brachial plexus injury, the Oberlin transfer coapts a redundant ulnar nerve fascicle to the biceps branch of the musculocutaneous nerve. Combined with a median fascicle to the brachialis branch, it restores elbow flexion faster than grafting from the root. This makes compartmental branch anatomy directly surgical.

keyPoints: Intermuscular septa divide the arm into anterior (flexor) and posterior (extensor) compartments
Anterior compartment: biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis, supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve
Posterior compartment: triceps brachii, supplied by the radial nerve
Brachial artery runs medially with the median nerve and divides into radial and ulnar arteries
Cubital fossa contents lateral to medial: (radial nerve), biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve
Radial nerve in the spiral groove is at risk in mid-shaft humeral fractures

test.q: Which nerve supplies the anterior compartment of the arm?
test.explain: The musculocutaneous nerve, from the lateral cord, supplies biceps, brachialis and coracobrachialis. The radial nerve supplies the posterior compartment of the arm. The axillary nerve supplies deltoid and teres minor. The ulnar nerve supplies no arm muscles.

test.q: Which muscle sits in the posterior compartment of the arm?
test.explain: Triceps brachii is the main posterior compartment muscle and extends the elbow.

test.q: Which muscle is the most powerful supinator of the flexed forearm?
test.explain: Biceps inserts on the radial tuberosity and rotates the radius, so it is the strongest supinator when the elbow is flexed. Brachialis inserts on the ulna and cannot supinate.

test.q: In the cubital fossa, which structure lies just medial to the brachial artery?
test.explain: From lateral to medial the order is biceps tendon, brachial artery, then median nerve (TAN).

test.q: The medial border of the cubital fossa is formed by:
test.explain: Pronator teres forms the medial border and brachioradialis the lateral border. Brachialis and supinator form the floor.

test.q: Where does the brachial artery usually divide into the radial and ulnar arteries?
test.explain: It ends in the cubital fossa. Teres major marks where the brachial artery begins.

test.q: Which nerve travels in the radial (spiral) groove of the humerus?
test.explain: The radial nerve runs with the profunda brachii artery in the spiral groove, so it is at risk in shaft fractures.

test.q: What lies superficial to the bicipital aponeurosis and is used for drawing blood?
test.explain: The median cubital vein crosses the roof of the fossa. The aponeurosis lies between it and the artery and median nerve.

test.q: Which arm muscle flexes the elbow in any forearm position?
test.explain: Brachialis inserts on the ulna, so forearm rotation does not affect it. Coracobrachialis acts at the shoulder.

test.q: The medial and lateral intermuscular ___ divide the arm into two compartments.
test.explain: These fascial sheets attach to the humerus and separate the flexor and extensor compartments.

test.q: What is the name of the triangular hollow in front of the elbow?
test.explain: The cubital fossa is bounded by pronator teres, brachioradialis and the line between the epicondyles.

test.q: Which artery travels with the radial nerve around the back of the humerus?
test.explain: The profunda brachii (deep artery of the arm) accompanies the radial nerve in the spiral groove.

kidTest.q: What do the front arm muscles mainly do?
kidTest.explain: Front muscles like the biceps bend your elbow.

kidTest.q: Which muscle straightens your elbow?
kidTest.explain: The triceps in the back room straightens the elbow.

kidTest.q: How many rooms is the upper arm split into?
kidTest.explain: There is a front room and a back room.

kidTest.q: What passes through the hollow at the elbow bend?
choices: A rib bone and a tooth root
A lung airway and a gland
kidTest.explain: A big artery and a nerve pass through to reach the forearm.

kidTest.q: The muscle you flex to show off is the b _ _ _ _ _ s.
kidTest.explain: The biceps is in the front room and bends the elbow.

advancedTest.q: A mid-shaft humeral fracture causes wrist drop but elbow extension is preserved. The best explanation is:
choices: Triceps is supplied mainly by the musculocutaneous nerve
Branches to the triceps heads often arise above the radial groove
Elbow extension is mainly driven by brachioradialis
The radial nerve lies on the medial side of the humerus mid-shaft
advancedTest.explain: Triceps branches commonly leave the radial nerve before it reaches the spiral groove, so injury there spares extension but not wrist extensors.

advancedTest.q: Why is the lateral part of brachialis often innervated by the radial nerve?
choices: The musculocutaneous nerve ends before reaching the elbow
It extends the elbow alongside the triceps and anconeus muscles
It borders dorsal territory in the ventral-dorsal limb split
It crosses the shoulder joint like the triceps long head
advancedTest.explain: Brachialis is a ventral (flexor) muscle. Its lateral strip lies against dorsal (posterior-division) territory near brachioradialis, so it often picks up radial nerve fibres. Some anatomists regard this strip as a dorsal-derived slip, but its border position is the shared explanation. The distractors are false. Brachialis flexes rather than extends the elbow. It does not cross the shoulder. The musculocutaneous nerve continues past the elbow as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

advancedTest.q: During anterior distal biceps repair, which nerve injury is most expected given the anatomy?
choices: Anterior interosseous nerve of the arm
Ulnar nerve at the medial epicondyle
Axillary nerve around the surgical neck
advancedTest.explain: The terminal musculocutaneous branch emerges lateral to the biceps tendon right in the surgical field. The ulnar and axillary nerves lie well away from it.

advancedTest.q: In an extension-type pediatric supracondylar fracture, which finding best fits median-side injury?
choices: Numbness over the little finger and clawing
Weakness of shoulder abduction past 15 degrees
Loss of the thumb-index 'OK' sign pinch
Inability to straighten the elbow against gravity
advancedTest.explain: The anteriorly displaced fragment threatens the median nerve and its anterior interosseous branch, which powers the thumb-index pinch. Little-finger numbness points to the ulnar nerve instead.
